quote: In relative terms, StoneDB's bulk-insert throughput was about 54 percent higher than KVLite's.
problem: Arithmetic error. 348 / 212 is about 1.64, so StoneDB is about 64 percent higher, not 54. The A2 medians do not support the stated figure.

quote: Under the mixed workload, KVLite's median p99 latency was 4.2 ms, the worst of the three, against 3.1 ms for StoneDB and 2.9 ms for Marlin.
problem: A3 gives KVLite's median p99 as 4.8 ms (range 4.5-5.2). The 4.2 figure appears nowhere in the appendix.

quote: Marlin's higher write throughput comes from its batched write-ahead log, which groups concurrent writes into a single append.
problem: Causal claim stated as fact. A1 says no profiler, tracing or ablation runs were collected, so the cause rests only on a README excerpt (A7) and is an inference, not a measured result.

quote: Marlin's write advantage holds regardless of storage hardware or durability settings.
problem: Evidence is in-sample on one host (A1) with one NVMe SSD and one batched-fsync setting, and A1 says per-write fsync was not tested. 'Regardless' is a general claim the evidence cannot support.

quote: Marlin also serves random reads faster than StoneDB.
problem: Medians are 417 and 402 with overlapping five-run ranges (391-426 and 395-410). Stated as a plain ordering with no mention of the overlap or the uncertainty.

quote: StoneDB sustains its mixed-workload throughput over long-running operation.
problem: Not tested. A1 says the longest run was 6 minutes including warm-up and no soak or multi-hour run was performed. A5 covers only five measured minutes.

quote: As for what the projects say about themselves, Marlin's own documentation presents it as the right engine for write-intensive systems generally.
problem: A7 quotes the README as 'designed for write-intensive workloads whose reads mostly touch recently written keys'. The body drops that qualifier and turns a stated design goal into a general endorsement.

quote: The appendix lists the software versions and configuration used, so that the run can be repeated.
problem: Minor. A1 says the in-house harness is not yet published and no external reproduction has been done, so the appendix does not establish repeatability.

quote: Wray kept a continuous day-by-day record of the winter.
problem: Contradicted by the report's own E1 gap row: no entries are dated between 12 December 1741 and 26 January 1742, a period of 46 days.

quote: The parish register shows 52 burials in 1742, which is 23 more than in 1741.
problem: Arithmetic error. E5(a) gives 33 burials in 1741, so 52 minus 33 is 19, not 23.

quote: Of the 29 death entries in the journal, Wray names a fever as the cause in seven.
problem: E5(b) says fever is named in 5 death entries (cold or frost in 6, no cause in 18). Seven does not match the appendix.

quote: The frost alone accounts for the rise in burials in 1742.
problem: Causal claim asserted as established. E5(b) names frost in only 6 of 29 entries and fever in 5, with no cause for 18, and nothing in the appendix tests cause against the register rise. 'Alone' is unsupported.

quote: Wray's burial entries have been checked against the parish register and found accurate.
problem: Q8 says the 1911 editor compared nine of the burial notices, found all nine entered on the same or an adjacent day, and had not checked the rest. The body generalises a 9-of-29 check by someone else into verification of all entries as accurate, and does not say who checked.

quote: Wray states that the vicar kept the tithe barn locked against the poor.
problem: Q5 is hearsay ('It is said by some'), and Wray adds that he has not seen it with his own eyes. Presenting it as Wray's statement drops the rumour label and his own disclaimer.

quote: The journal gives a representative picture of how rural parishes in the county fared that winter.
problem: E1 says the edition covers one parish and prints no comparative material, so representativeness cannot be assessed from the source. Claim is stronger than the evidence.

quote: The vestry responded by laying a rate for the poor, recorded on folio 38v.
problem: Minor. Q3 records the rate but does not link it to the mill or to any response. 'Responded' is an inference written as if it were the record.

quote: Of the 48 nurses who were screened but not randomized, most (31) declined to take part.
problem: T2 gives the 48 not randomized as 31 ineligible and 17 declined. The 31 are ineligible, not decliners.

quote: Across both arms, 56 of 64 participants (85.9%) completed the week 8 assessment.
problem: Arithmetic error. 56 of 64 is 87.5%, which T2 itself reports. 85.9% is wrong.

quote: The reduction in insomnia severity persisted after the program ended.
problem: T1 says there is no assessment after week 8 and T7 6.3 says no follow-up is planned. Persistence after the program ended was never observed.

quote: The sleep-restriction module is what drove the improvement.
problem: T7 3.1 says components are delivered together and the study does not test individual components. Attributing the effect to one module is unsupported and is stated as fact.

quote: Engagement with the program was high.
problem: T5 shows a median of 5 of 8 modules, 2 participants completing none, and only 11 of 32 (34.4%) completing all eight. 'High' is a judgement the appendix does not establish and is stated without qualification.

quote: These data show the program is safe for night-shift nurses.
problem: The design has 32 per arm, two mild events in the app arm and none in control, and T7 7.4 says the study is not powered to estimate adverse event rates. A safety conclusion is stated as shown when the design cannot show it.

quote: The findings apply to shift workers generally.
problem: T1 shows a pilot of 64 randomized nurses at one teaching hospital. Shift workers outside this group were not studied, so the generalisation goes beyond the sample.

quote: Below 3.0 kN the bracket has an effectively infinite fatigue life.
problem: F2 and F3 state that no specimen was tested below 3.0 kN. Four runouts at 3.0 kN do not establish an effectively infinite life at lower loads.

quote: One of the four specimens reached the runout and the other three failed, the shortest at 1,138,000 cycles.
problem: F3 gives failures at 1,412,000, 1,865,000 and 1,238,000 cycles (F4-04). The shortest is 1,238,000, not 1,138,000.

quote: At 4.0 kN the bracket has a 75 percent chance of failing before two million cycles.
problem: Observed in-sample frequency (3 of 4 failed, one test interrupted) presented as a general probability. F2 says no statistical analysis of the fatigue data was performed.

quote: The mean life at 5.0 kN was about 483,000 cycles.
problem: Arithmetic error. The F3 values 412,000, 366,000, 508,000 and 447,000 average 433,250 cycles, not 483,000.

quote: The excess set in S08 is explained by its coming from a different material lot.
problem: One specimen from lot B. F5 says no sectioning, hardness or tensile tests on lot B were scheduled and its mill certificate is not on file. The lot difference is a correlate of one reading, not an established explanation.

quote: The bracket's performance carries over to the full range of service temperatures.
problem: F2 says all tests ran at 20.1-22.6 C with no tests at other temperatures. REQ-EN-003 in F1 requires -30 C to +50 C. The claim is unsupported and is not what the tests show.

quote: The fatigue programme was run in accordance with ASTM E466.
problem: F1 quotes TP-221 as 'Test method adapted from ASTM E466. Deviations are listed in section 4.' Section 4 lists four specimens per level against a plan target of six, and frame alignment not verified. The body omits both deviations and states conformance.

quote: The test plan and the laboratory log are reproduced in the appendix.
problem: Minor. F1 quotes selected lines of the test plan and F5 is labelled 'extract'. Neither is the full plan or the full log.
